passage: The akhada in Sirsi opened at five, and Divyansh had been there every morning since Class 8. Tonight his father, Mohit, sat on the cot with his arms crossed. "Wrestling won't pay for anything. You will sit for the science stream." Divyansh's chest tightened. He wanted to shout, and he felt guilty for wanting to. Instead he opened his notebook. "Papa, here's my training schedule. Here are my district results. I'll study three hours after practice, and if I don't make the state team by next year, I'll take the science stream." Mohit was quiet for a long time, turning pages. "You wrote all this yourself?" he asked. "Yes." "We'll see," said Mohit, handing the book back, slower than he'd picked it up.

qa.q: What time did the akhada in Sirsi open?
What two feelings did Divyansh have when his father crossed his arms?
qa.a: Defiance and guilt. He wanted to shout but felt guilty for wanting to, so he chose a calm approach.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do that made his case stronger than shouting would have?
qa.a: He showed a plan: a training schedule, district results, promised study hours and a fallback of the science stream, rather than shouting or lying about his studies.

qa.q: How might Mohit be seeing Divyansh's notebook?
qa.a: As proof of real effort and seriousness. He was quiet for a long time, turned pages and asked if his son wrote it himself, so he may be starting to reconsider.

grounding: The protagonist insists on his own sporting path but brings a plan, proof of effort and a fallback instead of shouting.
